II.2 GENERIC and pre-GENERIC


GENERIC (the General Equation for Non-Equilibrium Reversible-Irreversible Coupling [28]), in its original form, is an additive combination of a Hamiltonian and a gradient flow. Symbolically, it extends (2) to




\dot{z}=A\,\mathrm{d}E+M\,\mathrm{d}S

(22)

where E=E(z) and S=S(z) are interpreted as energy and entropy functionals, with \mathrm{d}E and \mathrm{d}S the appropriate derivatives. A=A(z) is an antisymmetric operator while M=M(z) is a symmetric, non-negative definite operator. Finally, E,S,M,A are assumed to satisfy the orthogonality conditions




A\,\mathrm{d}S=0,\qquad M\,\mathrm{d}E=0

(23)

As a consequence, along the flow,




\displaystyle\dot{S}
\displaystyle=\mathrm{d}S\cdot A\,\mathrm{d}E+\mathrm{d}S\cdot M\,\mathrm{d}S=\mathrm{d}S\cdot M\,\mathrm{d}S\geq 0



\displaystyle\dot{E}
\displaystyle=\mathrm{d}E\cdot A\,\mathrm{d}E+\mathrm{d}E\cdot M\,\mathrm{d}S=0


In other terms, GENERIC characterizes a dynamics of return to equilibrium consisting of two orthogonal parts, the first being dissipative (the gradient flow along the entropy S), whereas the second is Hamiltonian and conserves the energy E.


We consider here a less constrained version of those equations, which can be seen as a precursor to GENERIC, which we call pre-GENERIC. It consists in renouncing to the existence of a conserved energy E, but instead considering a general flow {\mathcal{D}}J instead of A\,\mathrm{d}E,




\dot{z}={\mathcal{D}}J+M\,\mathrm{d}S,\qquad M=DXD^{\dagger}

(24)

with the operator {\mathcal{D}} acting on J, a given function of z, similar to (1), and
where the second part is the gradient flow of equation (2).
The first constraint in (23) can then be replaced by the less constraining orthogonality condition




{\mathcal{D}}J\cdot\mathrm{d}S=0

(25)

leading as before to the monotonicity of S.
The second constraint in (23), as well as the conservation resulting from it, are removed as unnecessary for the structure.
Like in the case of gradient flow, (pre-)GENERIC can and in fact should be extended to nonlinear flows (see also [33]) as




\dot{z}={\mathcal{D}}J+D~\partial\psi^{*}(D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S/2;z)

(26)

The monotonicity of the entropy follows as in (6),




\dot{S}=\mathrm{d}S\cdot{\mathcal{D}}J+2~\textrm{d}S/2\cdot D\partial\psi^{*}(D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S/2)\geq 0

(27)

Recognizing the structure (26) as the typical behavior unifying various types of relaxation to equilibrium is one of the main results of this paper.
The appeal of pre-GENERIC is twofold: first, as we will see, it appears in examples in a more natural and physical way than full GENERIC, which often requires adding extra variables to the models; secondly, as shown in [34], it turns out that the aforementioned extension is systematically possible, meaning that pre-GENERIC formally implies GENERIC. We are therefore mostly interested here in working with pre-GENERIC. In order to get the full GENERIC structure, we have to add an auxiliary scalar variable E to the system, in order to fix the two conditions that were not satisfied above. We refer to [35] for one systematic way to do that.



As before we now examine a few illustrative examples.


II.2.1 Example 4: underdamped diffusions


As shown in [35], the underdamped Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equation naturally gives rise to GENERIC and hence to a triple (J,M,S). It provides us with an opportunity to illustrate the formal notation of (24).



The variable z is, as in Example II.1.1 above, a time-dependent density \rho(q,p;t), but in its underdamped version, depending on positions q\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and momenta p\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equation is given by




\dot{\rho}=-\nabla_{q}\cdot\rho\frac{p}{m}+\nabla_{p}\cdot\rho\left(\nabla_{q}V+\nabla_{q}(\Phi\star\rho)+\gamma\frac{p}{m}\right)+\gamma\,\beta^{-1}\,\Delta_{p}\rho

(28)

for damping coefficient \gamma, mass m and inverse temperature \beta=(k_{B}T)^{-1}.
The convolution is defined as




\Phi\star\rho\;(q)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\Phi(q-q^{\prime})\,\rho(q^{\prime},p^{\prime})\,\textrm{d}q^{\prime}\,\textrm{d}p^{\prime}


That equation arises as a mean-field limit of underdamped diffusions interacting through a potential \Phi, with friction \gamma and at inverse temperature \beta [36]. The Kramers equation describing the evolution of a probability density for underdamped Markov diffusions is recovered for \Phi=0.



In order to unravel the structure of (28), we rewrite it in matrix form, separating the q and p directions. For instance, the operator D={\mathcal{D}} is given by minus the divergence




D=-\nabla=-\begin{bmatrix}~\nabla_{q}~&~\nabla_{p}~\end{bmatrix}

(29)

Moreover, this being an equilibrium system, we can define the Gibbs entropy




{\mathcal{S}}[\rho]=-k_{B}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\rho\log\rho\,\textrm{d}q\textrm{d}p

(30)

and the energy (including kinetic energy, potential self-energy and interaction energy)




{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\left(\frac{p^{2}}{2m}+V(q)+\frac{1}{2}(\psi\star\rho)(q)\right)\,\rho\,\textrm{d}q\textrm{d}p

(31)

and combine them into the free energy functional {\mathcal{F}}[\rho]={\mathcal{H}}[\rho]-T\,{\mathcal{S}}[\rho].


The equation (28) can be then written as




\dot{\rho}=-\nabla\cdot\rho K\,\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}+\nabla\cdot\chi\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{F}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}

(32)

with 2d\times 2d matrices




K=\begin{bmatrix}~~0~&~1~\\
-1~&~0~\end{bmatrix}~~~~~\mathrm{and}~~~~~\chi=\rho\gamma\begin{bmatrix}~0~&~0~\\
~0~&~1~\end{bmatrix}

(33)



The system evolution (32) (and thus also (28)) has the pre-GENERIC structure (24), with S=-{\mathcal{F}},M=-\nabla\cdot\chi\nabla, and with J=\rho K\,\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}. Indeed, as required for (27) we have the orthogonality




\displaystyle J\cdot D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S
\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}\nabla\cdot\rho K\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{F}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}\,\textrm{d}q\textrm{d}




\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}\nabla\cdot\rho K\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}\,\textrm{d}q\textrm{d}p-\beta^{-1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}\nabla\cdot\rho K\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{S}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}\,\textrm{d}q\textrm{d}p

(34)



\displaystyle=0


because of the antisymmetry of K for the first term, and the fact that \nabla\cdot\rho K\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{S}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}=(\nabla_{q}\nabla_{p}-\nabla_{p}\nabla_{q})\rho=0 for the second term in (34).



II.2.2 Example 5: Andersen thermostat


A good example of a nonlinear GENERIC system is the so-called Andersen thermostat [37], often used for numerical simulations of Hamiltonian systems subject to thermal fluctuations. In this model, independent massive particles with positions q and momenta p, of mass m and subject to a potential V(q), are perturbed in their Hamiltonian motion by having their momentum randomized according to their natural Maxwellian distribution at constant rate \varphi\geq 0. The evolution of the density of particles \rho is then given by




\dot{\rho}(q,p)=-\nabla\cdot\rho(q,p)K\,\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(q,p)}+\varphi\,\frac{e^{-\frac{p^{2}}{2m}}}{\sqrt{2\pi m}}\int\textrm{d}p^{\prime}~\rho(q,p^{\prime})-\varphi\,\rho(q,p)

(35)

which is a combination of a Hamiltonian flow and a jump process on p for inverse temperature \beta=1.
The Hamiltonian is given by




{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\left(\frac{p^{2}}{2m}+V(q)\right)\,\rho(q,p)\,\textrm{d}q\textrm{d}p


and the symplectic matrix K is the same as in (33). We can also use the same entropy \mathcal{S} and free energy \mathcal{F} as there.
For the jump part we imagine replacing all sums by integrals in Section II.1.2 getting a nonlinear gradient flow (26) with S=-\mathcal{F} and




\psi^{\star}(f;\rho)=\frac{2\varphi}{\sqrt{2\pi m}}\,\int e^{-\frac{p^{2}+p^{\prime 2}}{4m}}\,\sqrt{\rho(q,p)\rho(q,p^{\prime})}\left(\cosh f-1\right)\,\textrm{d}p\textrm{d}p^{\prime}

(36)

The corresponding negative divergence D and gradient D^{\dagger} are as in (11),




Db\,(p)=-\int b(p,p^{\prime})\,\textrm{d}p^{\prime},\qquad D^{\dagger}a(p,p^{\prime})=a(p^{\prime})-a(p)


That allows us to write (35) as




\dot{\rho}+\nabla\cdot J=D~\partial\psi^{*}(D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S/2;z)

(37)

which is of the pre-GENERIC form (26) with \mathcal{D}=-\nabla\cdot, and J=\rho K\,\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)} and the orthogonality (25) as before in (34).


This example can be easily extended to more general jumps and even to a combination of diffusions and jumps, as long as the rates satisfy detailed balance with respect to \mathcal{H}. This type of system was considered in [38] and interpreted as being in equilibrium with work-producing reservoirs, where it is necessary to factor out that work in order to obtain the physical entropy production of the system. As we see here, that is equivalent to writing the fluctuation symmetry around the average flux J present in the system.



II.2.3 Example 6: nonlinear friction


We continue with the jump part for (q,p)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2} but with transitions p\rightarrow p\pm N^{-1} with appropriately rescaled rates, by analogy with the Ehrenfest model in Section II.1.3. The backward generator A_{N} on any smooth function f is given by




\displaystyle A_{N}f(q,p)=
\displaystyle\left(\nabla f(q,p)\right)\cdot K\,\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}




\displaystyle+N\varphi~e^{-N\frac{(p+N^{-1})^{2}-p^{2}}{4m}}[f(q,p+N^{-1})-f(q,p)]




\displaystyle+N\varphi~e^{-N\frac{(p-N^{-1})^{2}-p^{2}}{4m}}[f(q,p-N^{-1})-f(q,p)]

(38)

Under the N\rightarrow\infty limit, that becomes




Af(q,p)=\left(\nabla f(q,p)\right)\cdot K\,\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}-2\varphi~\sinh\left(\frac{p}{2m}\right)\nabla_{p}f(q,p)


which corresponds to the equations of motion




\displaystyle\dot{q}
\displaystyle=\frac{p}{m}



\displaystyle\dot{p}
\displaystyle=-\nabla_{q}V(q)-2\varphi~\sinh\left(\frac{p}{2m}\right)

(39)

which shows nonlinear friction.
Defining the energy h(q,p)=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}+V(q), we can rewrite it as




\begin{bmatrix}\dot{q}\\
\dot{p}\end{bmatrix}=K\nabla h+\partial\psi^{\star}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\nabla h\right)

(40)

with




\psi^{\star}(f_{q},f_{p};q,p)=2\varphi\;\left(\cosh f_{p}-1\right)

(41)

which is of pre-GENERIC form (26) with D=\mathcal{D}=1, J=K\nabla h and S=-h. The orthogonality (25) is verified as




J\cdot D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S=-(K\nabla h)\cdot\nabla h=0

(42)

by the antisymmetry of K.

III.2 From generalized detailed balance to GENERIC


An essential ingredient in the previous analysis and examples was the (standard) condition of detailed balance (49). Looking back at the Examples II.2.1–II.2.3 for GENERIC flow we see that it is important to introduce momentum or velocity degrees of freedom to naturally give rise to the additional Hamiltonian flow. While such systems remain generalized reversible — one needs to flip the velocities when reversing the spatial trajectory — the condition (49) must be revisited.



Let us start with the constraint (44) on (45). We no longer require (49) but we suppose indeed that the Lagrangian satisfies




L(J-j;z)-L(J+j;z)=j\cdot D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S

(69)

for some function J(z), to be derived from the Lagrangian as well. The reasoning of section III.1 can then be repeated by replacing L with \tilde{L}(j;z)=L(J+j;z). The new Lagrangian \tilde{L} inherits the relevant properties of L: non-negativity, convexity in its first argument, and unique minimization. The Hamiltonian H is obtained as before in (46), but the generalized detailed balance condition (69) leads to a modified version of (50),




H(-D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S/2-f;z)-H(-D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S/2+f;z)=-2f\cdot J

(70)

making the duality between L and H more symmetric than before.


The functions \psi and \psi^{\star} are still defined as the re-centered symmetric parts of L and H, and are still Legendre transforms of one another. They verify




\displaystyle L(j;z)
\displaystyle=\psi(j-J;z)+\psi^{\star}(D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S/2;z)-\frac{1}{2}(j-J)\cdot D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S

(71)


\displaystyle H(f;z)
\displaystyle=\psi^{\star}(f+D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S/2;z)-\psi^{\star}(D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S/2;z)+f\cdot J

(72)

and the typical current j_{z} or zero-cost flow is given by




j_{z}=\partial H(0;z)=J+\partial\psi^{\star}(D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S/2;z)

(73)

Adding the orthogonality condition J\cdot D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S=0 leads naturally to the nonlinear version of pre-GENERIC, with \dot{z} given by (26) for \mathcal{D}=D,




\dot{z}=DJ+D\partial\psi^{\star}(D^{\dagger}\textrm{d}S/2;z)

(74)



We see next how that structure arises from the large deviations of the examples in Section II.2.


III.2.1 Example 4 bis: underdamped diffusions


Concerning the Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equation of Section II.2.1 we can use the fluctuation theory in [35]. We have a quadratic Lagrangian,




L(j;\rho)=(j-J)\cdot\frac{\chi^{-1}}{4}(j-J)-\frac{\textrm{d}S}{2}\cdot\nabla\chi\nabla\frac{\textrm{d}S}{2}-\frac{1}{2}j\cdot\nabla\textrm{d}S

(75)

with
Hamiltonian current,




J=\begin{bmatrix}\rho\frac{p}{m}\\
-\rho(\nabla_{q}V+\nabla_{q}\Phi\star\rho)\end{bmatrix}

(76)

The associated Hamiltonian to (75) is




H(f;\rho)=f\cdot\chi(f+\nabla\textrm{d}S)+f\cdot J

(77)

We thus recover the structure of (71) and (72), with the same functions \psi and \psi^{\star} as for the detailed balanced overdamped case in Section III.1.1:




\psi(j;\rho)=j\cdot\frac{\chi^{-1}}{4}j,\qquad\psi^{\star}(f;\rho)=f\cdot\chi f

(78)

from which the equation (32) derives its structure.



III.2.2 Example 5 bis: Andersen thermostat


We now consider N particles evolving according to the thermostat dynamics of Section II.2.2, i.e., according to (35). The only origin of randomness is the momentum resetting in the jump-part, while the Hamiltonian flow continues. We are therefore in the situation of (43) where J=\rho K\,\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)} is the Hamiltonian current corresponding to




\begin{bmatrix}\dot{q}\\
\dot{p}\end{bmatrix}=K\,\nabla\frac{\delta{\mathcal{H}}[\rho]}{\delta\rho(r)}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{p}{m}\\
-\nabla_{q}V(q)\end{bmatrix}

(79)

For (45) we only need to estimate the probability of Poisson-distributed jumps but that is the same as for the Markov jump processes in Section III.1.2. We thus have for the current j corresponding to the momentum jumps the expressions




\psi(j;\rho)=2\varphi\int\frac{e^{-\frac{p^{2}+p^{\prime 2}}{4m}}}{\sqrt{2\pi m}}\sqrt{\rho(q,p)\rho(q,p^{\prime})}\left(\lambda\left(\frac{\sqrt{2\pi m}e^{\frac{p^{2}+p^{\prime 2}}{4m}}j_{q,p;q,p^{\prime}}}{2\varphi\sqrt{\rho(q,p)\rho(q,p^{\prime})}}\right)+1\right)\,\textrm{d}p\textrm{d}p^{\prime}

(80)

and




\psi^{\star}(f;\rho)=2\varphi\int\frac{e^{-\frac{p^{2}+p^{\prime 2}}{4m}}}{2\sqrt{\pi m}}\sqrt{\rho(q,p)\rho(q,p^{\prime})}\left(\cosh f_{q,p;q,p^{\prime}}-1\right)\,\textrm{d}p\textrm{d}p^{\prime}

(81)

as before in (65).



III.2.3 Example 6 bis: nonlinear friction


In the example from Section II.2.3 we have \mathcal{D}=D=I and we are in the case with constraint (44) in (45). As in Section III.1.3, we can directly write the Lagrangian for the dynamics defined in (38), with a Hamiltonian flow and jumps of the form p\rightarrow p\pm N^{-1} at fixed q, with rates k^{\pm}(q,p)=N\varphi~e^{-N\frac{(p\pm N^{-1})^{2}-p^{2}}{4m}} :




L(\dot{q},\dot{p};q,p)=2\varphi~\lambda\!\left(\frac{\dot{p}+\nabla_{q}V(q)}{2\varphi}\right)+2\varphi~\cosh\!\left(\frac{p}{2m}\right)+\dot{p}\frac{p}{2m}

(82)

with constraint \dot{q}=\frac{p}{m} and \lambda as in (62). The associated Hamiltonian is




H(f_{q},f_{p};q,p)=2\varphi~\cosh\left(f_{p}+\frac{p}{2m}\right)-2\varphi~\cosh\!\left(\frac{p}{2m}\right)+f_{q}~\frac{p}{m}-f_{p}\nabla_{q}V(q)

(83)

These can be decomposed along equations (71) and (72), with functions




\psi(\dot{q},\dot{p};q,p)=2\varphi~\lambda\!\left(\frac{\dot{p}}{2\varphi}\right)+2\varphi~~~~\mathrm{and}~~~~\psi^{\star}(f_{q},f_{p};q,p)=2\varphi\left(\cosh f_{p}-1\right)

(84)

giving the required structure of (39).
